newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle brings new crewman for Mir station.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle brings new crewman for Mir station.

text.p: A four-month tour of duty aboard Russia's Mir space station ended on Wednesday for U.S. astronaut John Blaha.
The space shuttle Atlantis docked with Mir late on Tuesday to bring Blaha home, deliver supplies to the Mir crew and drop off Blaha's successor Jerry Linenger.

The change of shift aboard Mir officially occurred at 4:45 a.m. EST (0945 GMT) when Linenger's gear, including a specially moulded seat needed in case of an emergency return to Earth, was moved aboard the station.

The hatches between Atlantis and Mir had swung open about four hours earlier to ecstatic cheers from both crews. Communications problems had delayed the opening, to the frustration of the Mir crew, who eagerly beckoned for the shuttle crew to enter.
"Welcome! Welcome! Welcome!" an overjoyed Blaha shouted when the door finally opened. "Welcome to space station Mir."
"Home looks great," Linenger said as he floated through the maze of modules where he will live and work for the next four months.

Russia crewmen Valeri Korzun and Alexander Kaleri welcomed their visitors with a traditional Russian offering of bread and salt. It was the second time they had witnessed a shuttle docking as both were aboard the station when Atlantis arrived last September bringing Blaha to replace Shannon Lucid.
Blaha was unable to contain his excitement as he welcomed the Atlantis crew in the station's cramped docking module.
"This is kind of neat," he said. "Shuttles coming up here and docking and bringing stuff and people, and then shuttles leaving and taking stuff back down. We are truly in the space station business."

Atlantis and Mir linked up at 10:54 p.m. EST Tuesday (0354 GMT on Wednesday) as they orbited about 240 miles (386 km) above Russia, southeast of Moscow. It was the fifth time the shuttle had visited the station.

"Contact and capture," radioed Atlantis commander Mike Baker as the spaceships' metallic, petal-like docking rings joined. Electric motors drew the craft together, completing the docking process and making an air-tight seal. Atlantis and Mir had a combined mass of about 530,000 lbs (240,400 kg).
Blaha had watched the shuttle's arrival, his face pressed against a small porthole in the station's main module. "We see someone in the window of Mir with their thumb out," Baker reported.
"It's nice to see you guys," Blaha radioed later. "I saw you coming as a shining star."
Linenger's tour of duty aboard Mir will end in May, a month before his second child is due to be born. He will be the fourth U.S. astronaut to live aboard the station.
NASA scientists have devised a programme of more than 80 experiments for Linenger to perform but the highlight will be a six-hour spacewalk, the first by an American from Mir.

Atlantis was to remain docked with Mir for five days while the two crews moved a total of 5,975 lbs (2,710 kg) of supplies and equipment between the craft. Russian officials admitted their cash-strapped space programme now relies on the U.S. shuttle to ferry supplies to the station.

Blaha, an avid football fan, hoped to be back on Earth in time for the Super Bowl on Jan. 26, although his team, the Dallas Cowboys, would not be playing. Atlantis was scheduled to land at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre on Jan. 22.
